citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice, as used by the complete variational, Sobolev-extension and compact-spectral suppliers. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain. Define $H(\operatorname{curl})=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\in L^2\}$ and $H(\operatorname{div})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{div}u\in L^2\}$ with their graph norms, and let $X$ be the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the smooth fields on the closure with $n\times u=0$; this is an explicit weak perfect-electric-conductor boundary class. Put $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$ and $H=\overline{V}^{\,L^2}$. Then the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity tending to infinity whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and the zero eigenspace is finite dimensional and must be retained when the topology allows it. Each eigenfield $u_j\in V$ satisfies the full graph-class variational identity $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=\lambda_j\int_\Omega u_j\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$. The eigen equation is $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ distributionally with the PEC trace, and for every explicitly chosen mathematical speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and every initial displacement $q_0\in V$ and velocity $q_1\in H$, the associated second-order wave has coefficients $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with those initial coefficients. Its displacement lies in $C(\mathbb R;V)$ and its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$; finite modal sums converge respectively in $C(K;V)$ and $C(K;H)$ on every compact time interval $K$. The finite-dimensional $\lambda=0$ sector is retained with $a_j(t)=a_j(0)+ta_j'(0)$. This speed is a positive abstract mathematical parameter, not a physical constant or prerequisite. No identification with every maximal tangential-trace realisation, and no lossy, open or non-smooth-domain spectral claim, is made.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ in the graph sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]; connectedness is unnecessary. Write $H^m(\Omega)=W^{m,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with the multi-index integral norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) and $H_0^1(\Omega)$ for the $H^1$ closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). For every real $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ there is a unique $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^2(\Omega)$ satisfying

$$\int_\Omega(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+uv)=\int_\Omega fv\qquad(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

It satisfies $(1-\Delta)u=f$ distributionally and almost everywhere as an $L^2$ identity, and

$$\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad\|u\|_{H^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$

Moreover $D=\{\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega):\varphi|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$ is dense in $H^2(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega)$ in the $H^2$ norm: every such $w$ has $\varphi_j\in D$ with $\varphi_j\to w$ in $H^2$. Here smoothness on the closure means restriction of a smooth function on a neighbourhood of the closure, equivalently the smooth chart representatives used below. In particular $\nabla\varphi_j\to\nabla w$ in the graph norm of $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$, with zero curl and $\operatorname{div}\nabla w=\Delta w$; every $\nabla\varphi_j$ is smooth and PEC since its tangential derivatives vanish at the boundary. For precision, let $X_\Omega$ be the graph-norm closure of smooth vector fields on a neighbourhood of the closure with $\nu\times v=0$ on the boundary, where $\nu$ is the outward Euclidean unit normal. The ambient graph space consists of real $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_i\partial_iv_i$ and $\operatorname{curl}v=(\partial_2v_3-\partial_3v_2,\partial_3v_1-\partial_1v_3,\partial_1v_2-\partial_2v_1)$ lie in $L^2$; its norm squared is $\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2$. Thus $\nabla w$ belongs to this explicitly defined $X_\Omega$, the same completion used by the later cavity item. No equality with every maximal trace realisation is asserted.

No smoothness of $f$, no classical boundary value for general $u$, and no general nonsmooth-domain, Neumann, interface, or variable-coefficient claim is included. Zero boundary condition means membership in $H_0^1$; the published trace theorem identifies its trace as zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and $n\ge1$. In the proof write $e_n$
for the last canonical basis vector $e_{n-1}$. Let
$H=\mathbb R^{n-1}\times(0,\infty)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be the upper
half-space, written $x=(x',t)$ with $x'\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $t>0$. For every
$k\in\mathbb N_0$, every $1\le p\le\infty$ and every
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ there is a bounded linear extension
operator
$$E_{k,p}:W^{k,p}(H;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (E_{k,p}u)|_H=u\ \text{almost everywhere on }H .$$
For $k\ge1$ one may take, with the unique coefficients
$(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\mathbb R^k$ satisfying
$\sum_{j=1}^k a_j(-j)^m=1$ for $m=0,1,\dots,k-1$,
$$E_{k,p}u(x',t)=u(x',t)\ \ (t>0),\qquad E_{k,p}u(x',t)=\sum_{j=1}^k a_ju(x',-jt)\ \ (t<0),$$
and for $k=0$ one may take the even reflection
$E_{0,p}u(x',t)=u(x',|t|)$. In particular $H$ is a $W^{k,p}$-extension
domain in the sense of [[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]
for every $k$ and every $p$, and no density assertion is made or needed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ with
$M_\eta:=\|D\eta\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)}$ and compact support; the case
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is read by extending $\eta$ by zero.
Then for every $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and every $h\ne0$, on the shrunken set
$\Omega_{i,h}=\{x\in\Omega:x+he_i\in\Omega\}$ of
[[def-first-difference-quotient]] one has the exact identity
$$\delta_h^i(\eta u)-\eta\,\delta_h^iu=(\delta_h^i\eta)\,(\tau_{-he_i}u)\qquad\text{a.e. on }\Omega_{i,h},$$
where $\tau$ is the published translation $\tau_hu(x)=u(x-h)$ of
[[def-translation-of-a-function-on-rn]], so that
$(\tau_{-he_i}u)(x)=u(x+he_i)$. Consequently
$$\|\delta_h^i(\eta u)-\eta\,\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega_{i,h})}\le M_\eta\,\|\tau_{-he_i}u\|_{L^p(\Omega_{i,h})}\le M_\eta\,\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
and more generally, on the domain where both sides are defined,
$$\delta_h^i\big(\eta^2\delta_h^iu\big)=\eta^2\delta_h^i\delta_h^iu+(\delta_h^i\eta^2)\,(\tau_{-he_i}\delta_h^iu).$$
The statement is quantitative in $\|D\eta\|_{L^\infty}$ and does not assume
any regularity of $u$ beyond $W^{1,p}$.

**Sobolev multiplier and support facts used below.** For every integer
$m\ge0$, $q\in W^{m,\infty}(U)$ and $z\in H^m(U)$ on an open set $U$,
$qz\in H^m(U)$ and
$$D^\alpha(qz)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}{\alpha\choose\beta}(D^\beta q)D^{\alpha-\beta}z,\qquad |\alpha|\le m,$$
with $\|qz\|_{H^m(U)}\le C(n,m)\|q\|_{W^{m,\infty}(U)}\|z\|_{H^m(U)}$.
Also, every compactly supported $z\in H^m(U)$ lies in $H^m_0(U)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient

   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and $n\ge1$. In the proof write $e_n$
for the last canonical basis vector $e_{n-1}$. Let
$H=\mathbb R^{n-1}\times(0,\infty)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be the upper
half-space, written $x=(x',t)$ with $x'\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $t>0$. For every
$k\in\mathbb N_0$, every $1\le p\le\infty$ and every
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ there is a bounded linear extension
operator
$$E_{k,p}:W^{k,p}(H;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (E_{k,p}u)|_H=u\ \text{almost everywhere on }H .$$
For $k\ge1$ one may take, with the unique coefficients
$(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\mathbb R^k$ satisfying
$\sum_{j=1}^k a_j(-j)^m=1$ for $m=0,1,\dots,k-1$,
$$E_{k,p}u(x',t)=u(x',t)\ \ (t>0),\qquad E_{k,p}u(x',t)=\sum_{j=1}^k a_ju(x',-jt)\ \ (t<0),$$
and for $k=0$ one may take the even reflection
$E_{0,p}u(x',t)=u(x',|t|)$. In particular $H$ is a $W^{k,p}$-extension
domain in the sense of [[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]
for every $k$ and every $p$, and no density assertion is made or needed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a **bounded smooth graph domain**: a nonempty bounded open set such that for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and a function $h\in C^\infty(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,

$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\},$$

which is the $C^\infty$ case of the bounded $C^k$ graph domain of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open set with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$. Then there exists a real-linear operator $E_\Omega$, determined only by $\Omega$, a finite smooth atlas and fixed cutoffs, such that for every open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and every function $u:\Omega\times J\to\mathbb R$ that is of class $C^\infty$ on the open set $\Omega\times J$ and whose every mixed derivative $D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j u:\Omega\times J\to\mathbb R$ has a continuous extension to $\overline\Omega\times J$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), the function $E_\Omega u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times J$, satisfies $E_\Omega u(x,\tau)=u(x,\tau)$ for all $(x,\tau)\in\overline\Omega\times J$ and

for all multi-indices $\alpha$ and all $j\ge0$, and is spatially supported in one fixed compact subset of $V$, in the sense that there is a compact $K_\Omega\subseteq V$ with $E_\Omega u(x,\tau)=0$ for all $x\notin K_\Omega$, $\tau\in J$. For every compact $K\subseteq J$, every integer $m\ge0$ and every $j\ge0$,

$$\sup_{\tau\in K}\|\partial_\tau^j E_\Omega u(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_m\sup_{\tau\in K}\|\partial_\tau^j u(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\overline\Omega)},$$

citations.quote:
**Proper-graph branch.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory, put $\gamma(t):=(z(t),t)$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open with $\gamma[I]\subseteq\Omega$. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$ is **proper**: $\gamma^{-1}[K]$ is a compact subset of $I$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,$$

the second integral being componentwise, so $J=(J_1,J_2,J_3)$ is a triple of distributions, with components $\langle J_i,\psi\rangle=q\int_Iz_i'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. Then $\rho$ and $J$ are distributions on $\Omega$ ([[def-distribution]]) and, with the distributional derivative of [[def-distributional-derivative]],

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega).$$

Complex integrals mean $\int w:=\int\operatorname{Re}w+i\int\operatorname{Im}w$, with the same componentwise convention for improper limits. In formulas involving complex tests, $\langle u,w\rangle:=\sum_{j=1}^3u_jw_j$ for $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $w\in\mathbb C^3$, with no conjugation. This extends the real coordinate pairing; estimates on $J$ mean estimates on each component.

In the proper branch, an integral over $I$ means the proper integral over any compact subinterval containing the pulled-back support, with the integrand zero near its ends; additivity makes this independent of the subinterval. For $I=\varnothing$ both functionals are defined to be zero. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, and also if $I=\mathbb R$.

**Endpoint branch.** Suppose instead that $I=(a,b)$ is bounded with finite endpoints, that $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, that the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b\lVert z'(t)\rVert_2\,dt$ is finite, and that both endpoint events $(z(a),a)$ and $(z(b),b)$ belong to $\Omega$. Then the same formulas, with the integrals understood as improper integrals over $(a,b)$, define distributions $\rho$ and $J$ on $\Omega$, and

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\,\delta_{(z(b),b)},$$

the Dirac distributions being those of [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]].

Mere graph containment $\gamma[I]\subseteq\Omega$ does not make the pulled-back tests compactly supported, and it does not by itself give the source-free identity: in the endpoint branch the endpoint terms are present exactly as displayed, and they vanish on a test only when that test vanishes at the corresponding endpoint event. No Maxwell equation, no point self-force and no physical interpretation of $\rho$ or $J$ is asserted; only the distributional identities for the prescribed support are proved.

Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$, and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$, its derivatives are $\partial_t s=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the sphere and polar integrations below ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]). Let $c>0$, write $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, $\mathcal D:=\mathcal D(Q)$ for the test-function space of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], and $C:=\{(y,t)\in Q:t=|y|/c\}$ for the retarded cone. Define the functional $K$ on test functions by

$$\langle K,\psi\rangle:=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\psi(y,|y|/c)}{|y|}\,dy\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal D).$$

Then: (a) the integral converges absolutely for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$, the functional $K$ is a distribution on $Q$ ([[def-distribution]]), $(K,\psi)=0$ for every $\psi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap C=\varnothing$, and for every $(y_0,t_0)\in C$ and every neighbourhood $U$ of $(y_0,t_0)$ there is $\psi\in\mathcal D$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq U$ and $\langle K,\psi\rangle\ne0$; consequently $\operatorname{supp}K=C$. (b) For every $h\in C_c^\infty(Q)$ the function

$$(K*h)(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y,\,t-|x-y|/c)}{4\pi\,|x-y|}\,dy$$

is well defined (the integral converges absolutely), of class $C^\infty$ on $Q$, and for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$

$$\langle K*h,\psi\rangle=\langle h,\,K\circledast\psi\rangle,\qquad (K\circledast\psi)(y,s):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,s+\cdot)\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{\psi(y+z,s+|z|/c)}{|z|}\,dz;$$

moreover $W(K*h)=h$ on $Q$ in the classical pointwise sense, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is the wave expression of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. (c) Read $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ as the distributional operator built from [[def-distributional-derivative]]; then $WK=\delta_{(0,0)}$ in the sense of [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]], that is, $(WK)(\psi)=\psi(0,0)$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$. This identifies $K$ as the retarded fundamental solution of $W$; no smoothness of $K$ itself on the cone is asserted, and the advanced fundamental solution is not treated.

Let $c>0$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ be open. A **scalar-vector potential pair** of class $C^k$ on $\Omega$, for an integer $k\ge1$, is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ with $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ each of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], the components of $A$ being of class $C^k$ separately; the pair is **smooth** when both members are $C^\infty$, and **continuous**, or of class $C^0$, when both members are continuous. A pair defined on a set of the form $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $t_0<T$ is of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, **in the extension sense** when there are an open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ and a potential pair of class $C^k$ on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times J$ whose restriction to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ the given pair is; the same wording is used for $C^\infty$ and for the single functions $\varphi$ and $\chi$ below.

All operators $\nabla$, $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\Delta$ below act on the three spatial coordinates with $t$ fixed: for $\Omega_t:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:(x,t)\in\Omega\}$, apply the cited three-dimensional operators to the restrictions $x\mapsto\varphi(x,t)$, $x\mapsto A(x,t)$ or $x\mapsto u(x,t)$ on the open set $\Omega_t$. In particular $\nabla\varphi=(\partial_{x_1}\varphi,\partial_{x_2}\varphi,\partial_{x_3}\varphi)$ and $\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2u$; $\partial_t$ differentiates only the time coordinate.

For a potential pair of class $C^k$ with $k\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$.

For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function

$$G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,$$

also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega$ when $G(\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

For $k\ge2$ and a function $\chi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^k$, a **gauge function**, the **gauge transform** of the pair is

$$T_{\chi}(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$.

Finally, for a function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ put

$$Wu:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u,$$

with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\Box_c$ of the wave operator $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]. For a map $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ of class $C^2$ with components $U_1,\dots,U_m$, one writes $WU:=(WU_1,\dots,WU_m)$ componentwise.

Nothing in this definition asserts that a gauge function with prescribed auxiliary data exists, that every potential pair is gauge equivalent to a pair in Lorenz gauge, or that $Wu=g$ is solvable: those are conclusions with their own hypotheses. The signs $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $A+\nabla\chi$, the factor $c^{-2}$ in $G$, and the spelling *Lorenz* are part of the convention.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $m\ge1$, let U,V be open subsets of $\mathbb R^m$, and let $T:U\to V$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Borel $h:V\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_V h(y)\,dy=\int_U h(T(x))|\det DT(x)|\,dx$, with equality in $[0,\infty]$ and $0\cdot\infty=0$. This statement concerns Borel h; no completed-measurable substitution is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$

$$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$

If moreover $n=3$, then

$$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$

Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $\nabla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Since $z$ is $C^3$, it is $C^1$, and $I:=\mathbb R$ is open; the graph map $s\mapsto(z(s),s)$ into $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ is proper because a compact subset of $\Omega$ has bounded time coordinate, so its inverse image in $\mathbb R$ is closed and bounded. Hence [F1] applies with $q,\varepsilon_0$ as given: the functionals $\rho,J$ of the Statement are distributions on $\Omega$ and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$, which is (a).

Finiteness and bounds for the history pairings. Fix $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; by compactness of its support choose reals $M\ge0$ and $t_0\le t_1$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq\{(x,t):|x|\le M,\ t_0\le t\le t_1\}$, and put $A_\psi:=\sup|\psi|<\infty$, $Z:=|z(0)|$, $S:=\max\{0,(M+Z-ct_0)/(c-v_*)\}$, $H:=\max\{S,|t_1|\}$, $L:=1+M+Z+v_*H$, $T:=\max\{0,t_1+S\}$ and $M_Q:=T\sigma(S^2)L^2/(8\pi)$. If $g(s,w):=(z(s)+w,s+|w|/c)$ lies in $\operatorname{supp}\psi$, then $s\le t_1$; and for $s\le0$ the bound $|z(s)|\le Z+v_*|s|$ gives $t_0\le s+|w|/c\le-(1-v_*/c)|s|+(M+Z)/c$, so $s\ge-S$. Also $|w|\le M+|z(s)|\le M+Z+v_*H<L$. Therefore $\bigl|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle\bigr|\le\frac{|q|}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{-S}^{t_1}\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{B_L}\frac{A_\psi}{|w|}\,dw\,ds\le\frac{|q|M_Q A_\psi}{\varepsilon_0}$, and componentwise $\bigl|\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle\bigr|\le\mu_0|q|v_*M_Q A_\psi$. These bounds are fixed-support seminorms, so $\Phi$ and the components of $\Upsilon$ are distributions.

The retarded substitution map. Put $U:=\mathbb R\times(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, $V:=\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and $g(s,w):=(z(s)+w,\,s+|w|/c)$. Then $V$ is open: $\Gamma$ is closed, since a convergent sequence $(z(s_j),s_j)\to(x,t)$ has $s_j\to t$, hence $x=z(t)$ by continuity. The map $g:U\to V$ is a bijection with inverse $(x,t)\mapsto(s(x,t),x-z(s(x,t)))$: the root $s(x,t)$ of [F2] exists, satisfies $x-z(s)\ne0$ exactly off the worldline, and $s(x,t)$ is $C^1$ there because $z$ is $C^3$; conversely no image point lies on $\Gamma$, for $|w|=|z(t)-z(s)|\le v_*|t-s|=v_*|w|/c$ is impossible for $w\ne0$. The map is $C^1$ with derivative matrix (in the order $s,w_1,w_2,w_3$) whose last row is $(1,w/(c|w|))$ and whose first column is $(z'(s),1)$ with the identity in the remaining block; expanding along the last row gives $\det Dg(s,w)=-1+z'(s)\cdot w/(c|w|)=-\kappa(s,w)$, so $|\det Dg|=\kappa$, and $\kappa\ge1-v_*/c>0$ by [F2]. If $g(s,w)=g(s',w')$ then $|s-s'|=||w'|-|w||/c\le|z(s')-z(s)|/c\le(v_*/c)|s-s'|$, hence $s=s'$ and $w=w'$. By [F9], for every nonnegative Borel $h$ on $V$ one has $\int_Vh=\int_Uh(g)\kappa\,ds\,dw$, and for every $f\in L^1(V)$, $\int_Vf=\int_Uf(g)\kappa\,ds\,dw$.

Retarded derivative identities. On $V$, with $s=s(x,t)$ the root of [F2]: $s_t=1/\kappa$ and $
abla s=-n/(c\kappa)$. Hence $r_t=n\cdot(-z'(s)s_t)=-cN/\kappa$ and $
abla r=n/\kappa$; $R_t=-z'(s)s_t=-c eta/\kappa$ and $\partial_iR=e_i+ eta n_i/\kappa$; $ eta_t=\dot eta s_t=\dot eta/\kappa$ and $\partial_i eta=\dot eta\,\partial_is=-\dot eta n_i/(c\kappa)$. Since $\kappa=1-N$ and $D=\kappa r=r-R\cdot eta$, the product rules with the bilinearity of the inner product give $D_t=r_t-R_t\cdot eta-R\cdot eta_t=(c(| eta|^2-N)-rd)/\kappa$ and, componentwise, $\partial_iD=\partial_ir-(\partial_iR)\cdot eta-R\cdot\partial_i eta=n_i(1-| eta|^2+rd/c)/\kappa- eta_i$, that is, $
abla D= igl((1-| eta|^2+rd/c)/\kappa igr)n- eta$.

The needed triple-product identity follows directly from the coordinate definition in [F14]. For arbitrary $a,b,u\in\mathbb R^3$, the first component of $a\times(b\times u)$ is $a_2(b_1u_2-b_2u_1)-a_3(b_3u_1-b_1u_3)=b_1(a_2u_2+a_3u_3)-u_1(a_2b_2+a_3b_3)=b_1(a\cdot u)-u_1(a\cdot b)$, since the terms $b_1a_1u_1-u_1a_1b_1$ cancel. Cyclic permutation gives the other two components, so $a\times(b\times u)=b(a\cdot u)-u(a\cdot b)$. With $a=n$, $b=n-\beta$, $u=\dot\beta$ this gives $n\times((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta)=d(n-\beta)-\kappa\dot\beta$, since $n\cdot n=1$.

Scalar pairing identity. Insert the kernel identity [F3] into the definition of $\Phi$: $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\psi(g(s,w))|w|^{-1}\,dw\,ds$. The double integral is absolutely convergent by the cylinder estimate of step 1.2, so Fubini's theorem reorders it, and the substitution identity of step 1.3 for the $L^1$ function $\psi/(\kappa r)$ on $V$ (whose absolute integral is finite by the same cylinder estimate) turns it into $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_V\frac{C\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$, since $r(g(s,w))=|w|$, $\kappa(g(s,w))=\kappa(s,w)$ and the Jacobian factor $\kappa$ cancels $\kappa^{-1}$.

Vector pairing identity. Componentwise, $\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle=\frac{\mu_0q}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{\mathbb R^3}z_j'(s)\psi(g(s,w))|w|^{-1}\,dw\,ds$; the double integral is absolutely bounded by $\mu_0|q|v_*$ times the scalar majorant of step 1.2, Fubini applies, and the substitution of step 1.3 gives $\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle=\frac{\mu_0qc}{4\pi}\int_V\frac{\beta_j\psi}{\kappa r}\,dx\,dt$, where $\beta_j(s)=\beta_j(g(s,w))$ and $z_j'=c\beta_j$. Since $\frac{\mu_0qc}{4\pi}=\mu_0\varepsilon_0c\cdot\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=\frac{C}{c}\cdot c^2\mu_0\varepsilon_0=\frac{C}{c}$, this is $\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle=\int_V\frac{\beta_j(x,t)}{c}\frac{C\psi}{\kappa r}\,dx\,dt$.

Potentials and regular distributions. By [F2] the root is $C^3$ off the worldline, so $r,n$ are $C^3$, $\beta$ is $C^2$, $\kappa$ is $C^2$ and $D=\kappa r$ is $C^2$ with $D>0$ on $V$; hence $\varphi=C/D$ and $A=\beta\varphi/c$ are of class $C^2$ on $V$, and the identities of steps 2.1 and 2.2 read $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_V\varphi\psi$ and $\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle=\int_V A_j\psi$ for every test $\psi$. The graph $\Gamma$ is closed, hence Borel, and null: for each time $t$ its spatial section $\{z(t)\}$ is a singleton, so Tonelli together with the product identification of Euclidean measure gives $\lambda_4(\Gamma)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda_3(\{z(t)\})\,dt=0$. Therefore $\int_V\varphi\psi=\int_\Omega\widetilde\varphi\,\psi$ and $\int_VA_j\psi=\int_\Omega\widetilde A_j\psi$ for the zero extensions. Finally $\widetilde\varphi,\widetilde A$ are locally integrable: for a compact $Q\subseteq\Omega$ the substitution identity of step 1.3 and the cylinder bound of step 1.2 give $\int_\Omega|\widetilde\varphi|\mathbf 1_Q\le |C|\int_U\mathbf 1_Q(g)|w|^{-1}ds\,dw\le4\pi |C|\,M_{Q'}$ with $M_{Q'}=T'\sigma(S^2)L'^2/(8\pi)<\infty$ for the window constants of $Q$. Hence the regular functionals of $\widetilde\varphi,\widetilde A$ are distributions and $\Phi=u_{\widetilde\varphi}$, $\Upsilon=u_{\widetilde A}$.

The electric field. On $V$, $
abla\varphi=-C
abla D/D^2$, $\varphi_t=-CD_t/D^2$ and $A= eta\varphi/c$, so $A_t=(\dot eta\varphi/\kappa+ eta\varphi_t)/c=\dot eta C/(c\kappa D)- eta CD_t/(cD^2)$ and $E=-
abla\varphi-A_t= rac{C}{D^2} igl(
abla D+ rac{ eta D_t}{c} igr)- rac{C\dot eta}{c\kappa D}$. Substituting the identities of step 1.4, the bracket equals $ rac{1}{\kappa} igl(1-| eta|^2+ rac{rd}{c} igr)(n- eta)$, so $E=C rac{(1-| eta|^2)(n- eta)+rd(n- eta)/c}{\kappa^3r^2}- rac{C\dot eta}{c\kappa D}= rac{C}{\kappa^3r^2}\Bigl[(1-| eta|^2)(n- eta)+ rac{r}{c} igl(d(n- eta)-\kappa\dot eta igr)\Bigr]$, using $D=\kappa r$ to write the second summand over the common denominator. The cross-product identity $n	imes((n- eta)	imes\dot eta)=d(n- eta)-\kappa\dot eta$ of step 1.5 then gives the displayed electric field.

The magnetic field and regularity. By [F15] and the chain rule, $\operatorname{curl}A=
abla(\varphi/c)	imes eta+(\varphi/c)\operatorname{curl} eta$ with $\operatorname{curl} eta=
abla s	imes\dot eta$, so $\operatorname{curl}A=- rac{C
abla D	imes eta}{cD^2}- rac{C\,n	imes\dot eta}{c^2\kappa^2r}$. Substituting $
abla D$ from step 1.4 and using $n	imes(n- eta)=-n	imes eta$ gives $\operatorname{curl}A=-C igl[ rac{1-| eta|^2+rd/c}{c\kappa^3r^2}(n	imes eta)+ rac{n	imes\dot eta}{c^2\kappa^2r} igr]$. Crossing the field of step 4.1 with $n/c$ gives the same expression, because $n	imes n=0$, $n	imes(n- eta)=-n	imes eta$ and $n	imes(d(n- eta)-\kappa\dot eta)=-d(n	imes eta)-\kappa(n	imes\dot eta)$; hence $B=n	imes E/c$. Since for $z\in C^3$ the root is $C^3$ and $
abla D,D_t, eta,\dot eta,\kappa,r,n$ are as in step 1.4 with $\kappa r>0$ on $V$, both displayed fields are $C^1$ on $V$; the same computation with a $C^k$ trajectory uses the $C^k$ root branch of [F2] and gives $C^{k-2}$ fields, and the smooth branch gives smooth fields.
